items.stem: What can reasonably be inferred about why Mara asked contributors to describe where their plants had grown successfully?

choices: The restored reach contained finer gravel than upstream spawning beds, limiting the reproduction of species other than dace.

items.stimulus: When the city of Larkspur replaced a concrete bank along a 400-meter stream with soil, plants, and gravel, researchers compared the restored reach with a similar unrestored reach. Before the work, both reaches held mostly speckled dace and few other fish species. Two years later, dace counts in the restored reach were nearly twice their pre-project level, while the number of fish species had not changed; the control reach showed neither shift. The restored bank supported overhanging sedges that lowered midday water temperature, but its newly placed gravel was finer than the gravel in upstream spawning beds. During a drought in the third year, dace in the restored reach survived at higher rates than dace in the control, yet surveys still found no colonizing species. Water samples contained DNA from two fish species absent from net catches, although those traces appeared downstream as well. Because dace tolerate warm, slow water but the species detected through DNA require coarse gravel to reproduce, the team concluded that the project had improved refuge without yet creating conditions for a more varied breeding community. The researchers therefore recommended monitoring recruitment rather than treating a single season's DNA signal as evidence that restoration had already increased diversity.

items.stimulus:
Ecologist Mina Patel's team investigated whether rooftop gardens cool buildings mainly through their plants or through the water held in their soil. On each of three office buildings, the researchers installed two plots with identical plants and soil; one plot was watered every morning, while the other was watered only when its soil moisture dropped below a set threshold. For twenty cloudless afternoons, sensors recorded the temperature of each plot and of the uncovered roof beside it.

The daily-watered plots averaged 4.8 degrees Celsius cooler than the bare roofs, whereas the threshold-watered plots averaged 3.1 degrees cooler. The threshold plots used about 40 percent less water than the daily-watered plots, and they never became warmer than the uncovered roofs. Patel also found that plants in the threshold plots developed deeper roots during the study.

The results did not show that frequent watering was unnecessary: the daily-watered plots provided the greatest cooling, especially during extreme heat. They did suggest that a garden designed to conserve water could still provide meaningful relief from rooftop temperatures. Patel therefore proposed that building managers choose an irrigation schedule according to whether their priority was maximum cooling or a balance between cooling and water use.

items.stimulus:
At a coastal museum, conservator Lina Velez examined a 1930s mural whose dockworkers and cranes stood beneath an unusually pale sky. An archival photograph showed that the sky had once appeared darker. An infrared scan revealed boats sketched beneath the visible paint and several figures shifted from their original positions. Chemical tests found that the pale sky lay over a charcoal-gray wash, rather than over untouched plaster.

A letter does record that city officials objected to the mural's labor scenes, so the curator initially attributed the altered sky and missing boats to censorship. That explanation became less secure when scraping at two edge panels found the same pale layer beneath later varnish, in places where officials would have had little reason to intervene. Lina noted that the evidence could show a sequence of changes without showing why Chen made them.

Many interpreted the covered boats as proof that Chen had abandoned realism, while Lina argued that an underdrawing records possibilities, not necessarily a settled intention. items.stem: Which inference best reconciles the study's early difference in beetle abundance with its later difference in species richness?

items.stimulus:
Ecologists studied whether small islands of leaf litter could support ground beetles in city parks dominated by closely mowed grass. In eighteen parks, they paired similar plots and added a three-by-three-meter layer of leaves and fallen branches to one plot in each pair, while leaving the other plot bare and maintaining the same irrigation and mowing schedule. After six weeks, the litter plots contained more beetles, most of them belonging to two drought-tolerant species. By midsummer, however, the two kinds of plots held roughly equal numbers of beetles, although the litter plots contained 40 percent more species, including several rarely captured ones.

Because pitfall traps record movement as well as residence, the researchers could not assume that every beetle caught in a plot lived there. Most of the rare species appeared in traps only after rain, whereas the two common species were caught throughout the season. Temperature sensors showed that litter plots were cooler during the day and retained moisture longer after rainfall than bare plots. Across the parks, the litter treatment had its largest effect where lawns were frequently mowed and its smallest effect where shrub beds already stood nearby.

To distinguish attraction from retention, the team removed the litter from half of the experimental plots in autumn but left the surrounding vegetation unchanged, then sampled all plots the following spring. The cleared plots quickly returned to the bare plots' level of total captures, while maintained litter plots continued to contain more species. The researchers also found that the rare species reappeared in maintained plots after spring rains, even though the common species still accounted for most captures. They concluded that litter islands can provide temporary, connected patches of suitable conditions in otherwise uniform lawns, but that their value depends on repeated maintenance and does not make them a replacement for larger, more complex habitat.

items.stimulus:
Visitors to the 1931 Municipal Design Fair remembered the Pavilion of Echoes as austere: a low concrete room with no exhibits, labels, or visible machinery. items.stem: The final sentence most strongly suggests that, in Sato's view, a person's presence in the historical record depends not only on whether that person was observed but also on which of the following?
choices: Whether official proceedings contained more reliable information than everyday encounters.

items.stimulus:
When curator Nia Sato catalogued historian Elias Orne's notebooks, she noticed that his accounts of courthouse debates ran for pages, while reports by women market sellers appeared in only a few clipped phrases. Orne's contemporaries had praised him for giving town history a "plain" tone, and later scholars treated his unequal attention as proof that he considered official proceedings more historically valuable. Sato initially expected the marginalia to reveal Orne's private opinions, but found instead lists of sources, corrections of dates, and instructions to an apprentice named Lio. The notebooks therefore offered evidence of method more readily than of temperament.

A letter from Orne to Lio changes how the omissions can be read: Orne asks Lio to gather market testimony because Orne could not attend the morning market while consulting court ledgers. Lio's replies survive, but the summaries he sent do not; perhaps they were never copied into the notebooks, or perhaps a later editor removed them. Sato refuses to choose between these possibilities, since the physical record cannot show whether the missing accounts reflect an author's judgment, a division of labor, or simple loss. That restraint does not make her account indifferent; it marks the point at which interpretation would otherwise outrun evidence.

In her exhibition, Sato places the notebooks beside Orne's letters and the surviving fragments of Lio's correspondence. Her captions identify whose hand produced each passage and distinguish copied testimony from Orne's commentary, without claiming that either provides unmediated access to the past. Visitors are asked to notice not only who appears in a history, but which stages of its making determine who can appear at all.
